title: Integer Replacement
summary: Starting with a positive integer n, repeatedly apply the following operations: if n is even, divide it by two; if n is odd, either add one or subtract one.
statement: Starting with a positive integer n, repeatedly apply the following operations: if n is even, divide it by two; if n is odd, either add one or subtract one. Determine the least number of operations required to reduce n to one.
constraints: Even values must halve; odd values can increase or decrease by one. Count operations until reaching 1.
Intermediate values may exceed 2^31−1; Python integers support this.
hints: Even values have a forced next step. For odd values, consider the trailing binary digits.
Usually choose the neighbor that creates more trailing zeros, allowing repeated halving.
If even, halve. If n=3 or the low two bits are 01, subtract one; otherwise add one. Count each operation.
The value 3 is special because subtracting reaches 2 then 1. Near 2^31−1, adding one is valid and produces a power of two.
editorial: After an odd adjustment, at least one halving follows. Except at 3, an ending 01 favors subtracting and an ending 11 favors adding; this removes a run of low one-bits and creates more forced halvings. The special value 3 reaches the target sooner by subtracting. The independent oracle explores both allowed choices with breadth-first search instead of relying on this bit rule. Each constant-size group of operations shortens the bit length.

tests.explanation: Only halving is needed: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, for three operations.
Increasing first is better: 15 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 uses five operations; always decreasing would take six.
